prompt: [WP] The year is 2134. The human race, now almost entirely atheist, makes first contact with alien life and are greeted as the creatures created in God's image.
story:
Humanity has always been lonely. Looking, reaching, dreaming, striving for stars we might never reach. We never knew why. Perhaps it was simply some strange, unexplained compulsion pulling our eyes upward. Perhaps it was mere stubbornness which put the fire in our veins, and strength in weary arms. Perhaps all of it, from our solitude to our curiosity, to our very physical appearance was a coincidence. 

According to the aliens, it was not. 

'Made in God's image'. Words puzzled over, pored over, picked apart until interpretations abounded, and no mere man could hope to keep them straight. Words despaired over, dreamed over, driven until they were drivel, with no more discernable meaning than waves on the sand. 

Eventually, forgotten. Set aside, in favor of our new logic, with its sharp and bitter edges, and a world far larger than we could ever imagine; simultaneously too small for the one thing we could imagine, have imagined, perhaps, will always imagine: a Creator. Or, to some, we did not abandon our Creator. It was our Creator who abandoned us, leaving us to the tender mercies of a far too cruel world. 

Made in the image of God.

The words, foreign in that twisted alien tounge.  Assumed to be an error, a miscalculation. We spoke with the creatures. We spoke of their world, we spoke of ours. We spoke of space, glorious space. We spoke of danger, and beauty. When we had spoken until there was little left to speak of, we asked again. 

"What do you call us?"

"The Children of God."

To them, the question was simple. To us, anything but. How were we to learn? Who were we to tell? What celestial legacy are we to uphold? 

Made in the image of God.

Bittersweet.

story:
Every nation sent representatives, politicians and scientists and engineers and civic leaders, to Geneva, where the 3-day meeting was held. They argued about cost, about size, about materials. Plans were drawn and torn and re-imagined and negotiated. But finally, at the end of these harrowing 72 hours where few had slept much, a trajectory was mapped. It would be an enormous spacecraft, powered partly by solar and partly by nuclear fission, that would house all of humanity as the race sought a new celestial home. This project was going to be bigger, more expensive, and more collaborative than everything humanity had ever done, combined. It would be a truly Herculean effort.

And if you asked any philosopher, they would've shook their head and told you the truth of the future: that it was always doomed to fail.

The squabbles started almost immediately and never stopped. They spanned all corners of the imagination. Greedy politicians tried to squirrel away funds for themselves, thinking that the whole mission was pointless and that the Earth's imminent demise was a liberal hoax. Different groups of people fought tooth and nail to exclude other groups they did not like because they were Jewish or Muslim or Greek or Black or Trans or...well, every division of humanity had another counterpart hating their existence.

In all nations, work on the spacecraft went by in unsatisfying jolts and halts. Terrorist factions bombed factories, convinced that they were secretly making parts for a weapon that would be used by the country against whomever they didn't like. Scientists and engineers were kidnapped, tortured and murdered to impede the progress of this colossal waste of money.

Hundreds of millions of people worldwide, from politicians to the common salaryperson, loudly cried out against such acts, calling it suicidal on a species level.  But an equal number sneered and called them sheep, and worked ever harder to dismantle what they perceived to be yet another facet of elitist spending into useless projects that would not help the working class.

But soon enough, it all stopped. All of it. The Earth finally died, its oceans acidified and ambient temperatures too high to support macroscopic life. And all around the planet, in crumbling cities lay the skeletons of its once most sentient life-forms, gathered around the wholly incomplete sections of spacecraft.

The planet had become a tomb, and the half-built machines were the epithets.

story:
Sixteen generations. The guild had been around longer than that, but no single family had lasted so long. They were killed in battle, or by their own mounts. Sixteen generations, and all that weight on my shoulders as I watched the egg struggling to hatch.

We weren't allowed to help them. 

Everyone did, of course. I could see the others, crouched right up against their eggs, peeling at the shells. One was cut for his trouble, and promptly devoured by his hatchling. It charged toward the rest of us, and I stood still, like stone. They don't see so well as babies, only see motion. A second initiate was devoured before the Guildmaster got his beast down to stop it, pinning the hatchling under one giant, clawed hand and waiting to be told what to do.

My egg had stopped moving, the cracks still tiny and centered on a single point.

"This is why," the Guildmaster droned, you do not help them hatch.

Another hatchling burst free, knocking over his human in an effort to get up the speed to fly. Then the rest hatched out all at once, nearly a dozen little monsters, and they set to fighting each other.

Not mine. Maybe it had died. 

I pressed my lips together to keep from smiling. A dead dragon meant a new egg next season, a few months reprieve added to the years it would take for the beast to be big enough to carry me. No one would learn my secret fear.

But no, the egg resumed rocking, and the cracks started to widen.

I slowly fed my right arm through the harness, shaking it loosely to widen it, and then gripped the traces with the left. I had practiced this, hundreds or thousands of times, on horses and cows, and pigs, and even on the carved wooden face of a dragon that decorated the bannister of the family mansion. 

The egg toppled over, cracking nearly in half. The shell was broken, but the membrane inside still held it together and I watched my dragon - my dragon - use her front claws to shred it away and crawl free.

"Eyyyoh," I gave the traditional call, and when she swung her ugly head my way, I flapped my right hand, and she launched the way they always do. Last minute, I lifted my arm up, sliding it over her wet-slick face, and then yanked it away as I pulled hard on the traces.

She was caught, bridled as well as any new hatchling could have been, but I kept pulling, taking down to a knee in the hot sand to bring her off her feet and down onto her side, the way Grandfather had shown me. She lay for a second before trying to rise, and in that time I mostly managed to swing a leg over.

She couldn't carry me, not this young, but she still fought me like a demon, twisting and trying to bite and claw at me. I sat hard, my whole weight crushing her into the sand. *Sit her til she stops struggling* is what they said, so I sat, and tugged the traces side to side when her maw came too close to my knees.

It felt like ages before she was done, before I could stand on rubbery legs and lead her away, with only three others, the survivors of today's hatching, to the aerie. 

Sixteen generations. Gods damn it, I would have to fly.

"That is not a weapon! It's a murdering blight that needs to be ended." The Elf said with disbelief. The Dwarf laughed, "Reminds me of fine Dwarven technology. 'Cept that things only purpose is to kill."

Holding his massive palms forward. He opens one hand. "An Elven bow can hunt..." He opens up the next,"...and a Dwarven axe can chop through her enemies. That fricken thing just obliterates. Where is the hunt?! The thirst for battle?!"

"Can yall shut the f\*\*k up." I looked at them. It's a machine gun. I overexaggerated on the size and how much rounds it can actually shoot but in this world. Might as well be. "And give me back Sacha!"

I didn't wait for them to finish.

Before the Elf could retort I lunged at him.

"Bastard!" He hissed. Moving out the way from my dagger. I scowled. This isn't going to be easy. Physically, they outmatch me, that machine gun wasn't just an advantage over medieval tactics and weaponry. It also made up for many of my weaknesses defensively.

"It will never fall in the hands of evi-" The elf tried to finish before being interrupted by a large hammer appearing out of nowhere, unsettling the dust. "Ya can't talk to em! Them kinds don't take kindly to peaceful talks. A knock in the head outta get him to listen!"

The hammer shifted sideways and came at me at whirlwind speed.

"Nope!" I swung back in time. Getting my distance, I needed to counter. I bought a shield from the market before coming here to get Sacha. It laid on my back in case these guys got the jump on me before I did. Awkwardly enough, none of us have our weapon of choice ready since each of us had stolen ones weapon from another. I had no use for the Dwarven axe since I can barely lift it and the Dwarf is too clumsy to wield a bow.

Moving the shield to my forearm like a gauntlet, I could feel the weight weighing me down. Even this peasant shield is too much for me physically. Mind you, I'm pretty athletic in my world but in this one where there's barely any modern technology and people relied on magic rather than electricity. Everything is a little too heavy or not my size.

The dwarf swung again. I raised my hand just in time but not in time to brace for the impact.

The loud thundering sound of a metal clanging against metal almost numbed the pain that stretched across my hand. I couldn't move my shield. I felt my knees buckle against his massive strength. I can

[... DETERMINISTIC MIDDLE OMISSION ...]

ure here that we have never seen before. We may not have an opportunity to learn about this...this...hooman. To learn it's culture, religion, what it can eat, what it can-"

The dwarf look sheepishly at the Elf, already bored. "Yea, yea, just give me my axe back and I'll lock that devil weapon of 'is away and you and yours can take him and do whatever you want."

The Elf rolled his eyes. He quickly turned to his horse. The prized axe was tied to the massive stallion, still dwarfing it in comparison. But before he could unlatch the rope a loud bang is heard from the little human they thought they had beaten.

The Elf stood frozen. The single stream of blood trickling from the hole I put in between his head. It's lifeless body fell limp to the floor as the cold breeze of unknown horror crept on the Dwarf. Dwarves possess great courage but this time...for the first time... it wasn't his size that was the smallest.

I glared at the Dwarf with eyes that pierced his soul. His eyes darted to my hands. Impossible. I'm not supposed to have Sacha, "You two idiots forget one thing."

I stood up from my knelt position and aimed my revolver at my enemy.

"...A gunner never forgets his sidearm."

prompt: [WP] In 1954, major leaders of the world received a message: “We have examined your planet, and do not find it desirable. As we depart, we leave some of our technology knowledge on your moon for you.” They thought we’d all share it. Instead we had a space race, followed shortly by a tech revolution.
story:
They called it the technological revolution. 

Michael called it greed. 

And the rest of the world — well. The rest of the world was too consumed to even care. 

But Michael saw *them* for what they really were. Whoever they were. 

In the early 1950s, *they’d* left a message for all the major leaders of the world. *We have examined your planet, and do not find it desirable,* they said. *We leave some of our technology knowledge on your moon for you.* 

That was months ago. 

What followed was a rapid influx of technological growth, and of a space race that could only be called deadly. The technological revolution — abrupt and equally as deadly — was quickly replaced by the desire to replicate such technology. 

Michael had watched all this from his boxed television set, growing increasingly aware of the corroded feeling in his chest each time someone was announced dead, each time a war was declared, each time the technology was stolen. 

Still, it continued to make its rounds around the world, never in one country for too long and never with enough time to be studied. 

Never with enough time to be used. 

Michael didn't even know what this technology was, just that *they’d* created it and that it was special. Perhaps too special to be conceptualized. Surely too special to be shared. 

And maybe that’s what *they’d* expected, — whoever *they* were — that we’d share this gift — this disparity. That the world would be better for it. 

Clearly *they* didn’t know the human race. 

Clearly, *they* didn’t understand greed. 

Michael contemplated that, the idea of coming from somewhere that knows no avarice, of belong to a world of equitable universal law. Of giving away the very thing that set you apart. And most of all, of living without fear. 

He wondered if this world could ever be like that. 

Only, watching the men line up across from him, their uniforms pristine and tidy against such lanky and young skin, assault rifles tucked under their arms, the reflection of Michael’s eyes in their own — old and worn and already knowing such war — he knew it never would.

prompt: [WP] Hundreds of time travellers have gathered to watch the most important moment in human history. However, you, half naked and holding an empty bottle of beer, are wondering why all of these people are staring at you.
story:
The twilit sky gradually shrouding the surrounding cityscape in darkness was beautiful at this time of evening. From the park which was situated at the top of Rowley Hill near the city centre, I had a panoramic view of the entire city. There I sat, beer in hand, admiring the view.

Far within the distance, I saw rows of terraced housing dimly lit by streetlights which had just come on. Closer to the park itself was the Wills Tower; a tall skyscraper that towered over the central business district. Various floors of the building were lit up by interior lighting which shone out the windows whereas others - which were presumably vacant - were not.

It was truly a beautiful sight.

Turning to my left, I spotted a very large group of strange people. Some were dressed normally while others certainly seemed like they were not from around here. Their clothing seemed more... futuristic. What weirded me out the most was that they had been staring intently at me. What could they possibly want with me?

I turned my head and looked in every direction around me. There was certainly nothing going on around me that would warrant their gaze. What was going on?

Trying to ignore them, I turned back to stare at the city and took another sip of my beer when I spotted tiny specks of light moving through the roads. Although they were too far away to closely observe, it was clear to me that they were cars being driven by commuters trying to get home from work. There were so many of them, and it seemed that in parts of the city, the traffic was in gridlock.

Again I turned to my left and saw the same crowd staring at me. They must have been at it for a good few minutes now. Just what is going on here?

With hesitation, I stood up from my resting spot and walked further up the hill over to the group. One muttered "The saviour. He approaches." With every step I took towards the crowd, they began to disperse until I found myself running towards them. But they were faster than me and had been able to get away. By the time I reached the top of the hill, I truly saw the scale of how many people had come to stare at me. Just what the fuck was going on?

Feeling uncomfortable, I threw my empty beer can in the trash and walked away from the park. Not watching where I was going, I accidentally smacked into a woman. We both fell down with a thud.

"Hey, watch where you're going," she moaned.

"Sorry! I didn't see you there!"

prompt: [WP] Once again, you tried going on a date, they tried to sacrifice you, and your best friend ended up carrying you out after fighting their way in, shooting anything that moved. “I swear, I’m tempted to start dating you myself just so you can have at least one good experience.”
story:
"Deal." I said on her shoulder.
She shot another cultist.
"What?" she asked.
"I am thinking about a dinner at the Moving Cloud, you know, the restaurant built on the back of that Cloud Whale.
Then maybe a walk in Forbidden Forest." I said.
She just dodged an Arachnes web, shooting it straight in its head.
"You serious?" she asked putting me down, once outside.
I nodded.


"Well, this is my 10th date where I end up naked, with no action, only possible death, so yeah.
At least I know you won't try to sacrifice, eat me or lay eggs in me that will kill me." I laughed as we ran.
She stared back at me, slightly flushed, albeit it could be due to the fighting.
"Fine." she said.
I smiled.
"Tomight at 8?" I asked.
She nodded.
When we reached our town, we went our separate ways, and I prepared for the date.


In front of the small cloud that brings customers to the restaurant, I waited for her.
When she arrived, we both stared at each other.
She wore a fiery red dress, not her usual suit...
Damn, all that fighting made her a hidden Goddess, damn suits, hiding this sight.
"You are gorgeous." I said.
She was still staring at me.
Heh, I wore a golden dress hanging to its dear life, trying to hang on my body.
I dressed to impress.
"Shall we?" I asked.


We went up to the restaurant, and when we sat at our table she was still silent.
"Must you react like that?
You just carried me on your shoulder, while I was naked, like 10 hours ago." I giggled.
She downed a glass of wine.
"You look good too." she finally said totally blushed.
I smiled and we talked, the awkwardness slowly going away.
After the dinner, we walked in the forest, having a good time.
At some point we started holding hands.
"Yeah, if normal dates are like this, I can understand why people like them." I said.
She bit her lips, and got closer.
My heart threatened to explode...will we?
Then she pushed me down, as an arrow whooshed over us.


"Rawr." I said, nibbling on her ear, as she jumped up, and took off two daggers that were tied to her thighs.
"Alicia...you are cursed." she sighed, stabbing a man.
I watched her with a smile, realising I must have been in love with her for a while.
"At least you won't be bored, dating me." I said.
She groaned, yet didn't stop fighting, and protecting me.
My hero.

The boy smiles “A famous battle Operation Overlord happened here 300 years ago”. The vet replies “So I hear”.
story:
The boys father calls to him and he runs away after flashing another smile. He reminds me of the boy who waved from the bombed out balcony in Caretan. 

He reminds me of the family we found slaughtered outside of St. Lo. The body's of 2 young boys still wrapped in their mothers arms. All burned and black, but still in thos loving arms. I think of my own mother. How she must have wailed when they told her of my brothers passing on Guadalcanal. He was a tough bastard, but in the end the Nips won out. 

He reminds me of the boys I sat with on that Highins boat. All of us boys, in our own right. Children fighting a man's fight, for a man's cause. We became men on this sand. At least a few of us did. 

The Krauts were harder than whetstone. Especially those gunners. From the time we were within 40 yards of that beach the awful sound of Hitler's Buzzsaw never ceased. Even after we made it up the Point, that zipping sound rang in my ears. It still wakes me up at night almost 60 years later. For so long I tried like hell to keep thos thoughts from entering my mind. But today, I let them come back, today as I watched that French boy walk back to his family, I fell to my knees and cried. I cried 60 years of pain out in a matter of minutes. I let myself give way, and the floods poured out of my eyes for at least 10 minutes. 

When I felt my eyes start to dry I stood up. With all of the pride of the 2nd Rangers I stopped my shaking knees, and again looked over the once bloodied waters of the Channel. I closed my eyes and when they opened I saw my brothers standing before me. They looked as bright eyed and hopeful as the did that morning. Ray still had a piece of steak stuck in the hillbilly buck teeth. He grinned and saluted me once more. The boys had come to take me home. I closed my eyes and felt a peaceful ease washing over me. 

I thought it fitting that I should die, where I was born again.

prompt: [WP] "Warlocks don’t always make deals with demons; it’s more like a blanket term for anyone getting their magic in ways that wizards and sorcerers see as cheating"
story:
The warlock's hands hovered, as if hesitating, over the bundle of twisted roots and thorn-laced vines. She knew the sorcerers watched from their tower, high above in the smoke of their robes and the sharpness of their judgment. They whispered things like "false" and "unearned," though she never heard them directly. She felt it, though—the weight of their gazes, like shards of frost catching at the edge of her breath.


She pressed her fingers into the dark soil, her skin knowing the language of it without needing to speak. A slow breath escaped her lips, not in defiance, but something like it. **They called it cheating, this magic of hers. But she felt it more like breathing in reverse. A gift returned to the earth for a favor.**


The earth always whispers back.


What they didn’t understand, these men cloaked in their brittle robes of power, was that there are no straight lines in magic. No clean edges. **They wanted circles, symmetry. They wanted to pretend that magic could be confined to neat incantations and scripted runes, all inked onto spotless parchment.** As if ink were cleaner than blood.


But warlocks know better. They understand that magic curls and bends like the gnarled trees, **it finds the gaps in their precision, it seeps into the cracks between worlds**—not by force, but by invitation. Warlocks don’t make deals, they converse. With roots, with bones, with shadows that stretch longer than they should. They ask questions and they listen to the silences that follow.


“Demons?” She smiled at the thought, tasting the absurdity like iron in the back of her throat. No demons here. Just the ancient pull of something older than the books, **older than the ink they swore by.**


The vines in her hands twitched, came alive with a subtle hum. **Life stirs where the sorcerers see only decay.** This was not a pact, not some grand bargain struck in candle-lit chambers. It was simpler than that. A quiet exchange. Life for life, breath for breath. 


She stood slowly, the tangled mass now blooming at her touch, vibrant, pulsing. Power hummed through her fingertips, **but it wasn’t the kind that crackled or burned. It was the kind that grew.** Quietly. Slowly. It was power that sank into the earth and waited for spring.


The sorcerers would never understand that. **Their magic was something you could wear, parade around in a swirl of robes and gold-threaded hats.** Their spells shouted at the heavens, demanding to be seen. Hers whispered to the dirt beneath her feet, to the leaves that shivered in the wind.


They called it cheating because it wasn’t theirs, because they didn’t understand how magic could be something you *ask* for, rather than something you *take*.


She smiled again, this time to herself. Let them watch. Let them scoff and sneer from their towers. **Let them believe that power was something clean and separate from the world.**


She pressed her hand into the soil, deeper this time, her magic weaving into the roots, into the veins of the earth itself. She didn’t need their approval. She didn’t need their circles, their symmetry, their neat little definitions.


This was her magic. Twisted, wild, alive.


**Not stolen. Not cheated.**


Grown.

prompt: [IP] The Song of the Moon
story:
The moon beamed brightly behind him. He kept it to his back because it reminded him too much of her. Poor Charlie, only 10-years old and already he had seen more misery in his short life than most had in their entire lives. 

He played his guitar slowly, still learning how to play, but gaining progress. Originally, it sounded like metallic, garbled nonsense that had eventually turned into the simple songs he played ritualistically every night. Over the past two years since his sister's death, Charlie had come to this cobblestone border between his family's and his neighbor's farms.

Songs echoed across the dirt-landscape of the dusty, barren Texan Panhandle. Some nights would be played a happy jig as memories of his departed sister filled Charlie's head. Those were the nights he enjoyed, but most nights were like tonight; full of sorrow and anguish.

His songs, not so sweet now, were played roughly, angrily. Tears would spill from his eyes as he repeated over and over again, "It's not fair! It's not fair!"

And he played and played, releasing his emotion with each sour note plucked and each misplayed chord beaten out of his guitar. Tonight seemed like any other night, that is until his anger peaked and he swung his guitar - the last gift received from his talented sister - into the stone of the fence that separated his family's land and his neighbor's. It splintered violently, almost tearing the beaten instrument apart. Almost.

Charlie, who was breathing heavily, wiped away his tears, leaving stains that trailed down his cheek all the way to the neckline of his shirt. He lifted the guitar back into his view and noticed the new scar with wide eyes. A cracked line etched itself in the center of the guitar - in its heart, where the music came from. After examining the instrument for a short time and realizing what he had done, he quietly resumed his playing.

This time, he had left his steel pick behind and instead played softly with his fingers. The neighbor girl - Becky - heard the entire debacle, worried about Charlie. That is, until she heard the new song he was playing. It was sweet, soft, begging for forgiveness. It lulled the young girl to sleep, leaving the trace of a smile on her face.

Charlie's grandfather sat on the porch and looked on at the starry night. He hummed the familiar tune, recognizing it as one that Charlie's sister had played countless times before. Then, sharp, melodic whistles pierced his lips and bristled his moustache, joining the nocturne. 

And just as it had began, it had ended, the last of the notes echoing to the moon above. Finally Charlie looked to it, allowing himself to see it. With a smile and a final tear, he asked the moon:

"Did you hear my song, Lune?"

prompt: [WP] Write a story that involves a donkey, lime juice and aliens.
story:
"Just...just stop, man."

"Five more minutes, I swear!"

Rodney sighed, and kept an eye out for witnesses. Pablo was on his knees, and the silouette of his shadow stretched out, twitching across the desert landscape.

"Seriously, I don't--" Rodney took a pause to lick the cocaine residue off his palm, "--I don't wanna be out here when it gets dark.

"Don't be a pussy, Rod--nighttime ain't shit here compared to other star systems."

"Fuck off, it's not--fuck--you haven't heard it yet! There's something out there! Something dangerous!"

Blood covered Pablo's arms past his elbows, and traces surrounded him, appearing like dried rust in the sand. He pulled out a Parliament and loaded the filter. "Whatever. Anyways, I'm almost done."

"You said that an hour ago! We need to get back soon, either way! We're on a schedule!"

Pablo snorted a bump, lit his smoke, and shook his head. "Nah, nah, nahhh, man. We do shit for them all the time. ALLLL THE TIME. We deserve to enjoy some fun time everyonce in a while."

"This--this isn't fun! You always--"

"--just take another bump, dude! You'll feel better!"

"No!"

Pablo reached into his pocket, glanced past Rodney, and his eyes bulged as he screamed "WHAT IS THAT?!"

Rodney turned to look and had a fistful of coke slammed into his face.

"Wh-what the--NO! GODDAMNIT, PAB--NO!" 

He sneezed and attempted to wipe his face as Pablo cackled "you need to chill out! We're having a great time!"

"Ohh god, it's in my eyes..." He whimpered and fell beside Pablo, and immediately screamed in pain. 

"Hey, hey! I told you to stay clear of this!"

Rodney sniffled and pulled a couple of dirty syringes out of his arm, slouched in defeat-- "I'm done! We did our job! Let's get back to the base!"

"But I'm almost done!"

"No, you're not! This is impossible!"

"Well maybe if I had a few more rigs..."

"How about not?! Just-just explain--" he took a huge breath and steadied himself, "--just explain to me what it is you're trying to accomplish here."

"Okay. Okay, so--" Rod clapped his hands, rubbed them together and smirked, "Donkeys, they're pretty cool, right?" He paused a moment for reception, but continued. "And limes! They're pretty cool, too! Maybe not as noble as our friend here, *but*...but what if I told you...That together! Together they'd be... *even cooler*."

The sky began to bleed violet, and they both stared down at what laid at their feet. Pablo whistled in admiration. The creature was near perfectly splayed in half down the spine, with it's entrails still connected and folded into neat piles beside it. Surrounding it were multitudes of scattered squeezed limes and needles, clumps of sand clinging to them.

"Well, it's dead."

"You sure about that?" Pablo grinned.

Rodney glanced down, and reeled back in horror when he saw it's eyes shift towards him. Looking even closer he realized there was the slightest pulse, throbbing within the pile of organs.

A howl sounded off in the distance. And then a dozen more.

"The fuck is that?"
     
"That's what I was telling you about, man!"

*"No shit?"*

"No shit. You ready to go now?"

"Yeah, I suppose my work here is done." Pablo began to walk off.

"Wait! Aren't you going to, like--you know--put this thing out?"

Pablo took one last drag off his smoke and flicked the butt near his project. He gazed towards the animalistic cacophany of sounds in the distance.

"Nah, whatever *that* is, it'll take care of it."

prompt: [WP] You’ve reached a dead end in your journey. You’re ready to give up when your mysterious, ever-present guide appears. They reveal themselves to be none other than your future self.
story:
“Wait, you were me the whole time?” I stammered, looking at Miyu in confusion.

 “But, then why are you here? How? Where do I go next? Also, why are you a woman? When is that gonna happen to me? Aren’t you younger than me?”

My voice echoed throughout the empty building, bouncing off the dusty, disintegrating walls. Miyu put her hands on her hips and struck a pose with a bombastic “hmph!”, causing the various guns, knives, and gear to rattle as she started to answer me.

“Well, I’m from a different timeline a bit farther ahead than this one. I’m not younger than you, I just look like it due to anti-aging technology. I used a really expensive portal service to come here and help you save the people in this timeline. I studied all the prediction models so I could guide you, so here I am!”

Miyu, or me, grinned at me in satisfaction as I stared at her with a dumbfounded expression. Looking back at it now, it all made sense. No wonder she always had such an optimistic and cheery attitude despite the destruction of all civilization and humanity as I knew it. “Grandpa, I wanna go back to the house,” said Jenny. She crouched low to the ground to avoid any stray bullets. She hated when her parents left her with her grandfather.

“Push forward,” said her grandfather. “Don’t let them escape into the brush.” Jenny’s grandfather tripped on a tree root and smashed into the ground. He rolled over and rubbed the lump forming on his head.

“Grandpa.”

“Jenny? Is that you?” said her grandfather, his eyes still closed.

Jenny seized the opportunity. “Grandpa, we’re at the house. Remember?”

“Yeah, where’s that remote?”

The forest shrunk back into the floorboards. Jenny’s grandfather regained his plaid shirt.

Jenny kissed the banister. She popped up and then helped her grandfather to his feet.

“What do you say we go into the kitchen and I fix you a tuna sandwich?” said Jenny.

“Tuna? I haven’t had tuna since my days on the Pacific.”

The walls fell away to jumping white caps and the ceiling exploded into a torrential downpour. Within moments Jenny’s shirt was soaked through. The fishing vessel teetered like a drunk stumbling home. Jenny anchored herself to a support beam in the middle of the boat. Her grandfather rushed to the railing.

“Grab a line, boys!” he bellowed into the storm. “The night’s gonna take us to hell, but I’m not intending to check in.”

story:
“It’s not wise to let someone like that know your name,” Antony said, tapping out the bowl on his pipe. “You know I’ve told you that before.”

The boy rolled his eyes. “You tell me not to tell anyone my name. What makes her any different?”

Antony looked down his long, aquiline nose. His grey and wiry brows flexed above his eyes, bunching together into a look of concern. “She’s special.”

“I know,” the boy sighed. He looked down the road longingly where the woman had disappeared. “She was really something.”

Antony sighed as well, but the noise released from his lips was full of frustration rather than desire. He clucked his tongue at the boy. “Come now, Nathanial. I’ve taught you better than that.”

Nathanial silently kicked the dirt at his feet in response.

“Describe her to me. Show me what you’ve learned.” Antony began to pack his pipe.

“Well.” Nathanial’s brow furrowed as he concentrated. “She was tall. Brown hair. Wearing a red robe.”

“Cursory details, all of it,” Antony waved his hand in the air. “What else?”

Nathanial’s expression turned to a scowl. “Don’t rush me, Antony!”

Antony waggled the pipe stem at the boy. “If you want to improve, you’re going to have to work hard.”

“I know. Just give me a minute is all.” Nathanial was quiet.

“Close your eyes, Nathanial. Picture it in your mind. Tell me what you see.”

The boy obliged. “She was walking past the yard when she stopped. She leaned against the fence. Put her elbows up and leaned over.”

“And what got your attention then?”

Nathanial blushed. “She was beautiful. The way she leaned—”

“No, Nathanial. There is something else. Keep thinking.”

Nathanial thought hard. He saw her before him again, leaning over the fence. Her red robe slipped from one shoulder to expose bare skin, and the rest of the cloth draped around her body in tantalizing folds. Her hair was long and brown, curled in small, delicate ringlets. 

She had called out to him for a drink of water, and he drew up a bucket from the well. When he brought the bucket and ladle to her, she leaned forward, touching her lips to the ladle. As she did, the chain around her neck slipped loose from the folds of her robe, the pendant on it swinging forward. She caught it quickly, tucking it back under her robe.

Nathanial’s eyes snapped open. “The necklace. It had the mark.”

Antony nodded. “And who wears the mark?”

“Witches.” Nathanial looked down and kicked the dirt at his feet again.

“Yes, and if you hadn’t been so distracted by a bit of naked flesh, you might have thought twice before telling her your name.”

“But I only told her my common name, Antony!” Nathanial’s voice peaked into a sharp whine. “It wasn’t my secret name.”

“A name’s a name, boy, and you had best remember that if you want to learn magic.” Antony had finished packing his pipe and he lit it now, puffing slowly. When his match was exhausted and his pipe lit, he flicked the burnt tinder away. He held the pipe in his teeth as he rubbed a tattoo on his palm with the thumb of his opposite hand.

He nodded, though it was more to himself than to Nathanial. “Now go along inside and find the needle and thread. We need to weave you a protection ward.”

story:
"Are you sure we're going the right way, Master?" 

He tilted his head towards the stars. He eyed the leaf strewn path ahead. 

"Are you a scaredy cat my dear apprentice? Never fear, I'll protect y- ow!" 

He hopped on one leg, nursing his injured foot. His apprentice stalked ahead of him, her footsteps eating the ground quickly. 

"You're the one in need of protection!" she retorted, "This doesn't look like Niwa city at all!" 

He laughed sheepishly, drawing his cloak about him. 

"Maybe if you squint..." he tilted his head, staring at the ancient, vine-covered columns looming ahead of them. 

His apprentice let out an exasperated sigh, "How did you survive before I came along?" 

He shrugged, trailing after her. "Oh, somehow...life has a strange way of working out even after you think everything's gone horribly wrong." 

She cast him a look in the shadows of a half-broken stone roofing, "Are you trying to sound all old and wise again?" 

He chuckled, "Maybe." he tilted his head, allowing the darkness of the ancient structure to cover his face dramatically. 

Ah, would that it was sunset or sunrise instead of this indeterminate gathering gloom- he'd missed an opportunity there. 

Nonetheless. 

"I told you before, I'm older than I look." he said quietly, slipping past her and into the darkened interior. 

He struck a spark with a piece of flint, quickly assembling a makeshift torch. The interior of the ancient structure lit up in a flicker of flame and they stilled. 

"That's...kind of cool." his apprentice said, almost grudgingly as she stared at the gigantic stony statue of a sleeping, nine-tailed fox looming above them. She folded her arms and looked at him. When she realized he was just going to keep standing there gawking, she snatched the torch out of his hands and stepped further in. 

"After all this time..." 

His eyes glinted. His hand brushed against the stone fox and he felt for a brief instant- 

-warmth. 

The tattoos under his coat sizzled briefly. He shivered and moved away. 

"What are you mumbling about?" she asked, looking at him. 

"Nothing! Just...thinking about the city." 

She shot him a suspicious stare, "Are you alright? You're...distracted." 

He shrugged, hiding a wince as he felt *warmth*. 

"Did you know this used to be a temple?" he told her, "A fox worshipping temple. There was a fox spirit trapped here, legend said, and it'd lend its power to whoever offered it gifts." he chuckled, "Imagine that. Gifts from a cruel, twisted spirit." 

She looked at him, "You know all kinds of weird random stuff about the past, Master." 

"I suppose. They used to have a priest here too- a kitsunetsuki, the term was. He was supposed to seal away evil fox spirits in himself to free the possessed." 

She snorted, throwing down her pack on a relatively clear, dry area on the ground, "No one's stupid enough to agree to do that." 

He set down his pack nearby, relaxing on the floor against it. He looked at the large, still statue. 

"Right. No one..."

prompt: [IP] Construction of Space Station Zeta
story:
It was, at its heart, a construction site. On a pleasent, but otherwise unremarkable moon at the edge of the Sol system, humanity began to reach beyond their own solar system. They had mastered, quite well, the art of space travel through propulsion. They had colonized two planets and several moons, but it was with the Longhot project at Space Station Zeta where they aimed to travel to other solar systems and perhaps, one day, other galaxies. 

At the start of the project a Key Probe, as it was named, was fired off towards the nearest solar system, Alpha Centauri. The tiny probe was sped up to near light speed which gave the engineers around 4 years to complete the Gate. The Gate was to be twice as wide as today’s starships and consist of multiple operational points all linked together in a giant circle in orbit around the moon. 

The construction completed right on time, people had become very efficient at manufacturing and predictable projects were now the norm. Still, it was with no less excitement that the engineers and scientist prepared to open the gate, first of its kind, for the very first time. Central to the Gate and Key Probe was a complex pair of devices that each contained a quantumn computer and millions of individual electrons quantumnly entangled with a counterpart in the other device. If everything worked as planned, the two devices at precisely the same moment in time would each create a synchronized gravitational anomoly which, if the lab experiments scale to size properly, should open up a worm hole between the Key Probe and Gate. The Gate was designed to stabilize it.

The plan was to send in an exploration probe. If they had hit their mark their should be resources close enough to construct a second Gate on the other side. The scientists all seemed nervous about the return trip until another Gate was created to fully stabilize both ends. Until then, only probes would be sent back. 

Excidedly they prepared the observation probe. First of it’s kind and a point of pride, this probe would go further and faster than anything had been known to travel before. Next to the probe’s label, “LS01,” was the signatures of every engineer and scientist who has worked on the project. With the probe in place the team held their collective breaths and turned the gate on. The stars within the circle began to bend and shift as a gravitational lense formed from the distorting effects of... a worm hole! They had done it. It was, however, with great surprise that they saw several objects immediately begin to come through the gate. The objects paused in orbit outside the Gate momentarily then began approaching Space Station Zeta. Alarmed, the team feared the approach, but their feelings quickly turned to confusion. Visuals confirmed the objects were probes. Human made probes. The first one to land had clear markings, LS01. The signatures, their signatures, were sun-bleached, but visible. Next came LS02, LS03, and LS04. A dozen more were on approach. One scientist looked over at the brand new, one of a kind, LS01 they had prepared to launch and back to the identical probe that had just come out of the gate and landed at their station. In that moment he wondered exactly what it was that they had just created.
